# Rule-Based Logical Optimization {#sec-rule-based-optimization}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

The optimiser sits between the parser and the code generator. Its
job is to rewrite a logical plan into a better one. "Better" can mean
many things — fewer joins, smaller intermediate results, plans that
parallelise more naturally — but in NebulaStream it means something
quite specific.

NebulaStream's optimiser is *rule-based*: it applies a fixed
sequence of transformations, each a pure function from plan to
plan. There is no cost model, no plan-space exploration, no
estimation of cardinalities. Every query gets the same five rules
applied in the same order. The system Volcano [@volcano-paper] would
have called such a thing a "preprocessor" rather than an optimiser.

This chapter walks through that preprocessor. We will not pretend
it is more sophisticated than it is. The interesting part is not
the rules themselves — they are simple — but *why* the engine
chose simplicity here.

---

## 9.1 The five rules {#sec-five-rules}

The entry point is `QueryOptimizer::optimize`, in
`nes-query-optimizer/src/QueryOptimizer.cpp`. We saw it in
Chapter 2:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/src/QueryOptimizer.cpp
LogicalPlan QueryOptimizer::optimize(
    const LogicalPlan& plan,
    const QueryOptimizerConfiguration& defaultQueryOptimization)
{
    DecideJoinTypesRule joinTypeDecider(defaultQueryOptimization.joinStrategy);
    DecideMemoryLayoutRule memoryLayoutDecider;
    constexpr RedundantUnionRemovalRule redundantUnionRemovalRule{};
    constexpr RedundantProjectionRemovalRule redundantProjectionRemovalRule{};
    constexpr TypeInferenceRule typeInferenceRule{};

    auto optimizedPlan = LogicalPlan{plan};
    redundantProjectionRemovalRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    redundantUnionRemovalRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    typeInferenceRule.apply(optimizedPlan);
    optimizedPlan = joinTypeDecider.apply(optimizedPlan);
    optimizedPlan = memoryLayoutDecider.apply(optimizedPlan);
    return optimizedPlan;
}
```

Five rules, applied in order. The order matters — let us go
through them.

**1. RedundantProjectionRemoval.** A projection that selects every
field of its input in input order is a no-op. If the binder
produced one (and it often does, for the `SELECT *` shape), this
rule deletes it.

**2. RedundantUnionRemoval.** A union with one input is just that
input. Eliminate the union node.

**3. TypeInference.** Walk the plan and annotate every operator
with its input and output schema. This rule does not transform the
plan structurally; it decorates it. Subsequent rules and the lowering
phase rely on these annotations.

**4. DecideJoinTypes.** For each join in the plan, choose between
hash join, nested-loop join, and any future join implementation.
This is the most logically complex rule; we examine it in
@sec-join-decision.

**5. DecideMemoryLayout.** Choose row vs. columnar layout for each
operator's output. Currently always row (Chapter 4); the
infrastructure exists for future per-operator decisions.

That is all. No predicate pushdown. No projection pushdown. No
join reordering. No common-subexpression elimination. The optimiser
has no opinion on those questions.

---

## 9.2 Why no cost-based optimisation? {#sec-why-no-cbo}

Most relational databases have a cost-based optimiser. They have
one because a join over a billion rows of `customers` and a million
rows of `orders` can have wildly different costs depending on which
side is the build, whether indexes apply, and what predicates can
be pushed down. The optimiser's job is to navigate that
combinatorial space.

NebulaStream's workloads typically do not look like that. A
streaming query is small (tens of operators, not hundreds), shallow
(rarely more than two joins), and bounded in fan-out (the schemas
of streaming sources are usually narrow). The space the optimiser
would need to navigate is small enough that the right plan is
mostly the obvious plan.

There are also two specifically streaming reasons. First, statistics
are hard to maintain over an unbounded input — the cardinality
estimate for "the number of vehicles" is a moving target.
Second, the cost of a wrong plan is amortised over the query's
runtime; a streaming query running for a month will eventually
pay back any one-time optimisation overhead, but it will not
benefit from the optimiser re-considering after the workload
shifts (and re-considering during operation is its own problem,
as Chapter 22 discusses).

The pragmatic conclusion is that a rule-based preprocessor is
sufficient *for this engine, today*. As NebulaStream takes on
larger queries — multi-join analytical streams over many
heterogeneous sources — that conclusion may need to be revisited.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: when CBO matters"}
PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server invest heavily in cost-based
optimisation because their workloads include OLAP queries with
five-way joins and complex predicates. Apache Calcite provides
a CBO framework that Flink uses for its SQL surface.

Materialize uses no traditional CBO either, for similar reasons
to NebulaStream: streaming queries have less plan-space to
search, and the cost of a wrong plan is amortised. Hyper and
Umbra do CBO at runtime, recompiling when the cost model says a
better plan exists. NebulaStream sits at the simpler end of this
spectrum.
:::

## 9.3 The join-type decision {#sec-join-decision}

The most algorithmically interesting rule is `DecideJoinTypes`. It
inspects each `JoinLogicalOperator` and chooses an implementation
type, recording the decision in a `JoinImplementationTypeTrait`.

The current logic is structural rather than statistical. Look at
`DecideJoinTypesRule.cpp`:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/src/Rules/Static/DecideJoinTypesRule.cpp
bool shallUseHashJoin(const LogicalFunction& joinFunction)
{
    auto allowedLogicalFunction = [](const LogicalFunction& logicalFunction)
    {
        return logicalFunction.tryGetAs<AndLogicalFunction>().has_value()
            or logicalFunction.tryGetAs<EqualsLogicalFunction>().has_value()
            or logicalFunction.tryGetAs<OrLogicalFunction>().has_value()
            or logicalFunction.tryGetAs<FieldAccessLogicalFunction>().has_value();
    };
    // ... BFS traversal to verify all functions are allowed ...
    return true;  // Default to HashJoin if structure supports it
}
```

The question the rule answers is not "is hash join faster" but
"is hash join *applicable*." A hash join requires the predicate to
be a conjunction of equalities on field accesses; anything else
(a band predicate, an inequality, a UDF) forces the engine to fall
back to a nested-loop join.

The rule walks the join's predicate. If every leaf is a field
access and every internal node is `AND`, `OR` or `=`, the rule
flags the join for hash. Otherwise nested-loop.

This is a structural decision, not a cost decision. It is also the
right decision for the workloads NebulaStream targets: streaming
joins almost always *are* equi-joins on keyed fields, so the rule
chooses hash join almost always. The nested-loop fallback exists
for safety, not because anyone wants to use it.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 9.1: an inequality forces nested-loop"}
The query

```sql
SELECT * FROM trips JOIN tolls
  ON trips.gantry = tolls.gantry AND trips.timestamp BETWEEN tolls.start AND tolls.end
INTO billed_trips;
```

contains a `BETWEEN` predicate. The rule sees a `LessEquals` (or
similar inequality) leaf, finds it not in the allowed set, and
returns `false`. The join is tagged for nested-loop execution.

This will be slow on large inputs. A future optimiser would
recognise the band-join pattern and use a specialised
band-join algorithm (Chapter 22 mentions this as open work).
:::

---

## 9.4 Static vs. semantic rules {#sec-static-semantic}

The rules in `nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Static/` are *pure
syntactic* rewrites: they look at the plan structure and rewrite
it. They do not need to consult any external state. The five rules
called by `QueryOptimizer::optimize` are static rules.

There is also a directory `nes-query-optimizer/include/Rules/Semantic/`
containing rules like `TypeInferenceRule`,
`SourceInferenceRule`, `SinkBindingRule`, `OriginIdInferenceRule`.
These are typically called inside the binder (Chapter 5) rather
than the optimiser proper, because they consult the source/sink
catalog and the schema of catalog-resolved sources. The
distinction is more historical than principled — both are
plan-to-plan transformations — but it shows up in the directory
layout.

For our purposes, both kinds are "rules": pure functions that
transform the plan.

---

## 9.5 The trait set, revisited {#sec-trait-revisited}

We met the trait set in Chapter 6. Optimiser rules are the
principal users. Each rule attaches a trait to the operators it
touches, recording the decision the rule made:

| Rule | Trait it attaches |
|---|---|
| TypeInference | input/output schema annotations |
| OriginIdInference | `OriginIdTrait` per stateful operator |
| DecideJoinTypes | `JoinImplementationTypeTrait` |
| DecideMemoryLayout | `MemoryLayoutTrait` |

Downstream — particularly in the lowering phase (Chapter 10) —
the lowering rules read these traits to decide which physical
operator to instantiate. Hash-join build vs. nested-loop build is
one read of the join trait.

The trait pattern is what makes the optimiser composable. Each
rule is independent of the others; they communicate through
traits rather than through implicit structure. Adding a new rule
that attaches a new trait does not invalidate existing rules.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch9-summary}

NebulaStream's optimiser is a fixed sequence of five rules, applied
in order, each a pure function. There is no cost-based optimisation,
no plan-space exploration, and no statistics — a deliberate choice
matching the engine's typical workload of small, shallow streaming
queries. The most non-trivial rule, `DecideJoinTypes`, makes a
structural rather than statistical decision: hash join if the
predicate is an equi-join, nested-loop otherwise. Rules communicate
their decisions through a trait set attached to operators, which
the lowering phase (Chapter 10) reads to choose physical
implementations.

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch9-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 9.1: trace projection elimination"}
Add a `SELECT *` over a single source and run with TRACE
logging:

```sql
SELECT * FROM demo INTO result;
```

The binder produces a redundant identity projection. The
`RedundantProjectionRemovalRule` deletes it. Find the log line
that records the deletion. The plan after optimisation should
have one fewer operator than before.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 9.2: force a nested-loop join"}
Write a query whose join predicate is an inequality:

```sql
SELECT * FROM trips, gantries
  WHERE trips.coord_x BETWEEN gantries.x_min AND gantries.x_max
INTO matched;
```

Submit and observe the plan. The
`JoinImplementationTypeTrait` should be `NESTED_LOOP_JOIN`. What
is the runtime difference between this and an equi-join over
similar input? Run a benchmark to confirm.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 9.3: add a sixth rule"}
Sketch a `RedundantSelectionRemovalRule` that deletes a
selection whose predicate is a tautology (always true). Where
would it fit in `QueryOptimizer::optimize`? Which traits would
it preserve?
:::
